analysis.one_liner: Extends online privacy protections to teens and bans targeted ads aimed at kids and teens.
analysis.headline: A House subcommittee advanced the bill 14–10 on December 11, 2025; it now awaits action by the full Energy and Commerce Committee, with no floor vote in either chamber yet.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill updates the 1998 children's online privacy law to cover teens up to age 17, not just children under 13. It bans companies from using kids' and teens' personal data for targeted advertising, limits what data they can collect and how long they keep it, and gives parents and teens rights to see, correct, and delete that data. It also requires companies to secure minors' data, restricts sending it to foreign adversary countries without notice, and preempts state laws on the same subject.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 13 and teens aged 13–16, and their parents. Under the bill, large websites and apps could no longer build profiles on minors or serve them ads targeted at their personal data; parents of children and teens themselves would get direct notice of data practices and the right to delete, correct, and obtain the personal information collected about them. Schools could review and demand deletion of data collected on students. The FTC would also have to report annually on its enforcement of the law and, within three years, report on how the largest social media platforms comply [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Extends the reach of the 1998 Children's Online Privacy Protection Act from children under 13 to teens over 12 and under 17, so roughly 20 million more minors get legal protection of their personal data.

Makes it unlawful for covered websites and apps to collect, use, or share a child's or teen's personal information for individual-specific (targeted) advertising, while still allowing age-appropriate contextual ads.
Bars collecting personal information beyond what the service requires, bars keeping it longer than necessary, and requires operators to maintain reasonable security practices for minors' data.
Gives parents of children and teens themselves the rights to receive notice, obtain the data collected on them, delete it, refuse further collection, and challenge inaccuracies.
Expands the definition of personal information to include geolocation, photos and video, IP addresses, biometric data such as facial templates and voice prints, and DNA information.
Restricts storing, transferring, or giving foreign adversary ('covered') nations access to minors' personal information unless the parent or teen is notified.

Requires the FTC to report annually on its enforcement actions and investigations under the law, and within three years to report on how 'high-impact social media companies' — those with $3 billion or more in revenue and 300 million or more monthly users — comply.

analysis.who_pays: Large websites, apps, social media platforms, and the digital advertising ecosystem built on their data. Platforms would lose the ability to target ads at minors using their personal profiles, would face limits on data collection and retention, would need consent flows and deletion and correction systems, and would face FTC scrutiny and mandatory reporting — including annual public disclosure of enforcement activity and a compliance report on the biggest platforms. Companies would also bear the cost of compliance and the risk of FTC or state enforcement actions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media and ad-tech companies

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state law: no state could 'maintain, enforce, prescribe, or continue in effect any law... that relates to the provisions of this Act.' States that have passed their own — potentially stronger — rules for kids' or teens' online data could see them wiped out by a federal floor that only covers children under 17 and only online services within this law's scope.

Teens aged 13–16 can authorize the collection of their own personal information themselves; a parent's consent is required only for children. Some parents' groups object that this leaves the majority of minors' data collection subject only to a teen's own click-through consent, plus notice to the parent.

The bill lets schools consent on a student's behalf to edtech companies' collection of personal data, in place of parental consent, as long as the data is limited to educational purposes and parents get notice on request — which shifts authority from parents to school administrators for a large share of the apps children actually use.
The bill exempts tax-exempt 501(c)(3) nonprofits from the definition of an operator, so a tax-exempt site or app could collect minors' data outside these rules.

Enforcement runs through the FTC and state attorneys general; the bill's text creates no private right of action, so individual families would depend on federal and state agencies to pursue violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections are real and aimed at a widely acknowledged harm: companies profiling minors and monetizing their data through targeted ads. Extending the law to teens closes the largest gap in the 1998 statute, and the deletion, correction, and access rights are meaningful. The bill is imperfect in ways its supporters should acknowledge: federal preemption could extinguish stronger state rules, teens' self-consent weakens parental control for the 13–16 age group, and the school-consent pathway moves authority over student data from parents to school districts. On balance, a parent of a minor is considerably better off under this bill than under current law, provided the FTC enforces it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee on a 14–10 vote on December 11, 2025, and is waiting for the full committee to act; neither the House floor nor the Senate has touched it.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg (R-MI), joined by Rep. Laurel Lee (R-FL), introduced the bill on November 25, 2025, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
It was then referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade, which held a markup session on December 11, 2025.
On that same day, the subcommittee forwarded the bill to the full committee by a vote of 14 to 10.
No full committee vote, House floor vote, or Senate action has taken place, and Congress remains in session through January 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has become law, large social media platforms and ad-tech companies remain better off for now: they continue collecting and monetizing minors' data under the narrower 1998 rules, which apply only to children under 13, and they face no new limits on targeted advertising to teens.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large platforms and ad-tech firms, so far

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and cosponsor are both Republicans, and the subcommittee advanced the bill 14–10, but the record does not break down that vote by party and no floor votes have occurred.

industries.industry: Large social media platforms (Meta, YouTube, TikTok and similar 'high-impact' companies)
industries.note: These companies make money by profiling users and selling targeted ads. The bill bans targeted ads to minors, limits data collection and retention, gives families deletion rights, and subjects the largest platforms to mandatory FTC compliance reporting — costs that land directly on their core advertising business.

Ad networks and data brokers would lose access to minors' personal information for profiling and individual-specific advertising, though contextual advertising and audience measurement remain permitted.

The bill creates a school-consent pathway: edtech operators with written agreements with school districts can collect student data without parental consent, as long as it is limited to educational purposes. That locks in edtech's role in classrooms while imposing notice, deletion, and review obligations.
The bill exempts 501(c)(3) organizations from the definition of operator, freeing tax-exempt websites and apps from these restrictions while commercial competitors remain covered.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared only the first procedural step: subcommittee approval by a 14–10 vote on December 11, 2025. Next it would need a full Energy and Commerce Committee markup, a House floor vote, and Senate passage — a sequence that children's online privacy bills have repeatedly failed to complete in recent Congresses even with more cosponsors. With only two Republican sponsors so far and a divided subcommittee vote, the most likely path is that it waits in the full committee, and its fate depends on whether leadership schedules it before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
